papers.title: Which Past Matters? Training History and Multi-Forecast Horizon in Equity Transformers
papers.abstract: More historical data can improve estimation while introducing relationships that transfer poorly to current market conditions. We therefore examine how training quantity and historical selection interact with forecast horizon in intraday equity prediction. We deploy twelve configurations which combine four sampling and validation policies with 6, 12 and 24 month training quantities under a fixed cross-sectional Transformer and feature set. A monthly walk-forward experiment produces 264 refits and eight cumulative return forecasts from 5 to 120 minutes. Evaluation covers January 2025 through 20 October 2026 and uses cross-sectional Spearman information coefficients against future five-factor residual returns. Six-month recency sampling leads individual models at 5-15 minutes, while multi recency configurations lead at 20-30 minutes and uniform configurations at 60-120 minutes. Increasing training quantity does not uniformly improve accuracy while an equal-weight ensemble of all twelve models exceeds every individual mean at 15, 20 and 25 minutes, but not at the remaining horizons. These findings support evaluating historical selection jointly with forecast horizon without identifying a universal policy or a causal benefit from recency.

papers.title: On the use of case estimate and transactional payment data in neural networks for individual loss reserving
papers.abstract: The use of neural networks trained on individual claims data has become increasingly popular in the actuarial reserving literature. We consider how to best input historical payment data in neural network models. Additionally, case estimates are also available in the format of a time series, and we extend our analysis to assessing their predictive power. In this paper, we compare a feed-forward neural network trained on summarised transactions to a recurrent neural network equipped to analyse a claim's entire payment history and/or case estimate development history. We draw conclusions from training and comparing the performance of the models on multiple, comparable highly complex datasets simulated from SPLICE (Avanzi, Taylor and Wang, 2023). In environments where covariate data is limited, we find evidence that case estimates will improve predictions substantially, but that equipping the neural network with memory only leads to meagre improvements. Although the case estimation process and quality will vary significantly between insurers, we provide a standardised methodology for assessing their value.

papers.title: Covariate-Indexed Inclusion Probabilities on Unbalanced Panels
papers.abstract: We estimate the probability that an item with given covariates belongs to a set when the cross-section changes over time and items and periods are dependent. We propose two convex models whose fitted probabilities are nonnegative by construction and remain valid whatever the dependence between items, for which we establish consistency, finite-sample bounds and limit distributions for serially dependent panels. One suits events of moderate or high probability, the other rare events, and half the disagreement between their fits estimates a lower bound on the misspecification error of the worse fit, without knowledge of the true probabilities. On monthly US stock failures, the rare-event model predicts better than the ordinary logit and the classical failure logit. With the eight classical predictors, most of the gain comes from basis functions of the rank angle of each predictor and summary.
